title: Moore administration official backed for inspector general job, despite Republican protest vote
summary: A handful of Senate Republicans cast a symbolic protest vote Monday against the appointment of a Moore administration attorney to the job of inspector general for education, saying they concerned about her closeness to the administration.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 9, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters March 9, 2026

A handful of Senate Republicans engaged in a symbolic protest vote Monday in opposition to the appointment of a Moore administration attorney to the soon-to-be-vacant job of inspector general for education.

With Republicans holding just four seats on the 19-member Senate Executive Nominations Committee — and with one of the GOP members absent — Senate Minority Whip Sen. Justin Ready (R-Frederick and Carroll) acknowledged that the vote against Natalia Ahn was merely a protest vote. But he said Republicans are concerned that the inspector general should not be so closely tied to the administration she will be keeping tabs on.

“The governor appoints the board of education. They hired … the superintendent,” Ready said. “Now the governor is appointing the IG who worked for  him. It just feels like there ought to be a little more independence, separation.”

Ready said the vote “was the only thing we [Republicans] have to send a message that things are wrong.”

“The nominee herself is not so much the issue,” Ready said. “I think she’s qualified in a number of ways.”

Ahn is deputy legal counsel to Gov. Wes Moore (D), a position she has held for over three years. She also served three years as general counsel to the Montgomery County Public School system and spent nearly seven years as an assistant U.S. attorney in the District of Columbia.

A spokesperson for Moore, pointing to Ahn’s experience with schools and government, called the Republican complaints “deeply unserious.”

“The Office of the Inspector General for Education is an independent state office charged with investigating school systems and education entities across Maryland, and that independence is expected and respected,” said Ammar Moussa, the spokesperson, in an emailed statement. “If any matter were to present a conflict, Ms. Ahn would do what ethics rules require: recuse herself and refer the matter appropriately.”

The position is not appointed solely by the governor. The nominee for inspector general for education is chosen by a three-member panel that includes the governor, the attorney general and the state treasurer.

MDOT nominee on hold, Moore officially on ballot, Ellis is present, and not, more political notes

If approved by the full Senate, which is expected, Ahn would become just the second person to serve as inspector general since the job was created in 2019.

Richard Henry, who leaves the position in April, was picked by Gov. Larry Hogan (R) and two Democrats — Attorney General Brian Frosh and Treasurer Nancy Kopp. All three are now retired.

Henry founded the office that includes more than a dozen investigators and auditors. His term expired last summer. Henry has remained in the position since and re-applied for the job but was not selected to continue for a second term.

Ahn, appearing before the committee Monday night, said her vision for approaching investigations focuses on “working collaboratively to find solutions with the shared goal of improving schools and ensuring that our tax dollars are used in ways that do one thing, and that’s improve the systems that we all rely on.”

She compared her philosophy to Kintsugi, a Japanese art form in which broken pottery is repaired. Broken pieces are joined together in a decorative fashion that restores the item and highlights the imperfections.

Ahn said she became aware of the process as she recovers from a recent car accident that injured her right leg and requires her to use a scooter for mobility while she heals.

“It’s a practice where broken pottery is repaired, not with glue, but with a gold or silver lacquer to highlight, instead of hide the broken areas,” Ahn told the committee. “The idea is to preserve the history of the object carefully, carefully and meticulously put those pieces back together and highlight the cracks instead of hide them. And the point of this is so that the imperfection is embraced and the pottery is reinforced to make it stronger.

“If I am fortunate enough to be appointed, my goal is to deeply understand where there may be cracks in the system so we can highlight them and make our school system stronger,” Ahn said.

Still, Ready said he and other Republicans were concerned about Ahn’s past employment as it relates to her future position.

“She does have a good resume. I think we need to send a message that things are going to change,” he said. “I think it would be better to have something that looks arm’s length.”

— This story was updated on Tuesday, March 10, to include comment from the governor’s office.
